title: Simplification of linear expressions
summary: Simplify linear expressions by applying the distributive law, resolving nested brackets and managing fractional coefficients.
objectives: Distribute positive and negative factors to every term in a bracket.
Simplify nested and fractional linear expressions in a reliable order.
Recognise when terms cannot be combined and verify equivalence by substitution.

sections.title: Apply the distributive law to every term

blocks.text: A factor outside a bracket multiplies every term inside. Preserve each internal sign while multiplying coefficients and variable parts. A negative outside factor reverses the sign of every resulting term, not only the first.

After expanding all required brackets, collect like terms. Expansion changes the form of an expression but not its value. It is often helpful to write one multiplication arrow or intermediate product for each bracket term before simplifying.

blocks.text: For nested brackets, simplify the innermost group first when this reduces the work, then distribute the next factor. A minus sign immediately before a bracket is multiplication by −1. With fractions, decide whether the denominator divides one term or a complete numerator before doing any cancellation.

Fractional coefficients follow the same distributive law: one half of (6x − 8) is 3x − 4. Do not cancel across addition or subtraction. Cancellation is division of common factors in a product, so a common factor must first be visible in every numerator term.

blocks.text: An expression is simplified when the requested brackets have been expanded, numerical fractions reduced, and all like terms combined. Unlike terms such as 3x and 4, or 2x and 5x², must remain separate. A shorter-looking expression is not automatically equivalent if an operation has been lost.

Use structure and substitution together as checks. First verify each distribution algebraically. Then substitute a value such as x = 0 or x = 2 into the original and final forms. A mismatch identifies an error in signs, a missed bracket term or an invalid combination.
